p.seg: 〈Rén Běn〉
1 "Rén Běn"
In ancient times, rén (仁, benevolence) was taken as the foundation.
To govern with yì (義, righteousness) was called correctness (zhèng 正).
If correctness does not achieve its aim, then resort to expedient measures (quán 權).
Expedient measures originate from warfare,
and do not originate from ordinary people.
Therefore, to kill people, or to pacify people,
killing them is permissible.
To attack their state, or to love their people,
attacking it is permissible.
To stop war with war,
even warring is permissible.
Therefore, rén (仁) is seen as something to be close to,
yì (義) is seen as something to be pleased with,
wisdom (zhì 智) is seen as something to rely on,
and courage (yǒng 勇) is seen as something to devote oneself to.
trustworthiness is seen in faith.
Gaining affection within is
how to defend.
Gaining awe without is
how to wage war.
The way of war:
do not go against the seasons,
do not add to the people's suffering;
this is how to love our people.
Do not increase bereavement,
do not take advantage of misfortune;
this is how to love their people.
Do not raise armies in winter or summer;
this is how to universally love the people.
Therefore, even if a state is large,
being fond of war will surely lead to its demise;
even if the world is at peace,
forgetting war will surely lead to danger.
When the world is already at peace,
and the world is greatly joyful,
(conduct) *chūn wéi* in spring and *qiū miǎn* in autumn.
The feudal lords drilled their troops in the spring
and reviewed them in the autumn;
this was so they would not forget war.
In ancient times, chasing fugitives did not exceed one hundred paces,
and granting quarter did not exceed three *shè*;
this was to make clear their propriety.
Not pressing those who were incapable and showing compassion for the wounded and sick
was to make clear their righteousness.
Forming ranks before drumming
was to make clear their trustworthiness.
Contending for righteousness and not contending for profit
was to make clear their righteousness.
Being able to relinquish submission
was to make clear their courage.
Knowing the end and knowing the beginning
was to make clear their wisdom.
These six virtues, combined with timely teachings,
served as the guiding principles for the people;
this has been the policy since ancient times.
The governance of the former kings
followed the Dao of Heaven,
established the suitability of the land,
and governed the virtues of officials and the people,
thereby rectifying names and governing things.
Establishing the state and distinguishing duties,
distributing emoluments according to rank,
The feudal lords were pleased and submitted,
those from beyond the seas came to pledge allegiance;
lawsuits ceased and weapons were put to rest –
this is the governance of a sage's virtue.
Next in order,
wise kings established rites, music, laws, and standards,
and then created the five punishments to restrain the people from wickedness;
and then raised armored soldiers to punish injustice.
To inspect and hunt was to gather the feudal lords,
and to examine differences.
If there were times when someone disobeyed orders, disrupted norms, turned their back on virtue, and acted contrary to Heaven,
and endangered meritorious rulers,
a general announcement was made to the feudal lords,
clearly exposing the crimes,
and then it was announced to the August Heaven, Supreme God,
the sun, moon, and stars.
Prayers were offered to Hòutǔ (后土), the gods of the Four Seas, and the spirits of mountains, rivers, ancestral mounds, and local deities.
Then a report was made to the former kings,
and then the Grand Steward (zhǒngzǎi 冢宰) summoned troops from the feudal lords, saying:
"Such-and-such a state has acted against the Way,
let us punish it."
"On such-and-such a date, the army will arrive at such-and-such a state
to join the Son of Heaven in enacting just punishment."
The Grand Steward and the officials issued orders to the army, saying:
"Upon entering the land of the guilty,
do not desecrate the spirits,
Do not engage in unrestrained hunting;
do not destroy earthen fortifications;
do not burn walls and houses;
do not cut down forests;
do not seize domestic animals, crops, or tools.
If you see the old or young,
respectfully return them without harming them.
Even if you encounter strong individuals,
do not haggle or oppose them.
If you injure them in battle,
provide medical care and return them home."
After punishing the guilty,
the king and the various lords should rectify their states,
promote the worthy and establish the wise,
correctly restore their duties.
The ways in which a king or hegemon governs the lords are six:
using land to control the lords;
using policies and laws to regulate the lords;
using rituals and trustworthiness to befriend the lords;
using resources and strength to persuade the lords;
using strategists to maintain the lords;
using weapons and armor to subdue the lords.
Share worries and benefits to unite the lords,
and compare small matters to great ones to harmonize the lords.
There are nine cases for summoning a meeting to issue prohibitions:
if the strong bully the weak, then reprimand them;
If the treacherous and wise harm the people, then punish them;
If the violent internally oppress externally, then attack them;
If the fields are desolate and the people scattered, then reduce them;
If they rely on fortifications and refuse to submit, then invade them;
If they treacherously kill their relatives, then rectify them;
If they abandon and murder their ruler, then utterly destroy them;
If they violate commands and encroach upon governance, then block them;
If internally and externally there is chaos, and they behave like beasts, then exterminate them.
<The Meaning of the Son of Heaven>
2 The Meaning of the Son of Heaven
The meaning of the Son of Heaven,
must purely take as its model Heaven and Earth,
and observe the former sages.
The meaning of the scholars and commoners,
must be devoted to parents and be corrected by lords and elders.
Therefore, even if there is a wise ruler,
if the scholars are not first taught,
they cannot be employed.
In ancient times, teaching the people necessarily established the proper hierarchical relationships between the noble and the lowly,
so that they would not encroach upon each other;
virtue and righteousness would not surpass each other;
talents and skills would not overshadow each other;
courage and strength would not violate each other.
Therefore, strength was the same, but intentions were harmonious.
In ancient times, the decorum of the state did not enter the army,
and the decorum of the army did not enter the state,
Therefore, virtue and righteousness do not surpass each other.
The ruler values scholars who do not boast.
Scholars who do not boast
are instruments of the ruler.
If one does not boast,
then one has no desires.
If one has no desires, then one does not contend.
The judgments within the country
will surely attain the truth of the matter.
The judgments within the military
will surely attain what is appropriate.
Therefore, talents and skills do not conceal each other.
Obeying orders is rewarded with the highest honor for soldiers.
Disobeying orders is punished with the highest execution for soldiers.
Therefore, courage and strength do not offend each other.
Having fully imparted instruction to the people,
then carefully select and employ them.
When affairs are extremely well managed, then all the officials will be well provided for.
When instruction is extremely simple, then the people will cultivate goodness.
When habits are formed, then the people will conform to customs.
This is the ultimate in education and transformation.
In ancient times, chasing fugitives was not done at great distances,
and letting them go loosely was not permitted.
Not at great distances meant it was difficult to entice them.
Not letting them go loosely meant it was difficult to trap them.
Security was based on ritual propriety,
and victory was based on benevolence.
After victory,
its teachings can be restored,
therefore, the superior man values it.
Yǒu Yú Shì (有虞氏) issued proclamations within the state,
desiring the people to embody its commands.
The Xià Hòu Shì (夏后氏) made oaths in the army,
desiring the people to first accomplish its plans.
The Yīn (殷) made oaths outside the army gate,
desiring the people to first understand the intent and then act accordingly.
The Zhōu (周) swore oaths just before the blades clashed,
to unite the will of the people.
The Xià Hòu Shì (夏后氏) rectified its virtue,
not yet using the blade of war,
therefore its army was not mixed.
The Yīn (殷),
was righteous,
and began to use the blade of war.
The Zhōu (周),
was forceful,
and fully used the blade of war.
The Xià (夏) rewarded at court,
valuing goodness.
The Yīn (殷) executed in the marketplace,
to awe those who were not good.
The Zhōu (周) rewarded at court,
and executed in the marketplace,
encouraging the superior man,
and instilling fear in the petty man.
The three kings displayed their virtue,
as one and the same.
An army that is not mixed is not advantageous,
using long weapons for defense.
and short weapons for guarding.
If they are too long, it is difficult to attack with them;
if they are too short, they cannot reach.
If they are too light, they are sharp;
if they are sharp, they are easily disordered.
If they are too heavy, they are dull;
if they are dull, they are ineffective.
War chariots:
The Xiàhòu Shì 夏后氏 called them "hook chariots,"
prioritizing correctness.
The Yīn 殷 called them "respectful chariots,"
prioritizing speed.
The Zhōu 周 called them "primary war chariots,"
prioritizing goodness.
Flags:
The Xiàhòu Shì 夏后氏 used black heads,
symbolizing the people's holding [of power].
The Yīn 殷 used white,
the meaning of heaven.
The Zhōu 周 used yellow,
the way of earth.
Chapter,
The Xiàhòu shì 夏后氏 (Xia Dynasty) used the sun and moon,
valuing brightness.
The Yin (Shang Dynasty) used the tiger,
meaning the Bai Rong (White Rong people).
The Zhou used the dragon,
valuing refinement.
If the army focuses too much on power, the people will be suppressed;
if it focuses too little on power, the people will not be able to cope.
If the ruler causes the people to not obtain their righteousness,
the common people to not obtain their order,
skills to not be used to their advantage,
oxen and horses to not be able to bear their burdens,
and the officials to oppress them,
this is called too much power;
with too much power, the people will be suppressed.
If the ruler does not respect virtue but employs deceit and wickedness,
does not respect the Way but employs bravery and strength,
does not value obedience but values disobedience,
does not value good conduct but values violent conduct,
and the officials oppress them,
this is called too little power;
with too little power, the people will not be able to cope.
In military campaigns, relaxation (shū) is of primary importance;
with relaxation, the people's strength will be sufficient.
Even when engaging in battle with drawn blades,
foot soldiers do not rush,
The chariots did not race;
chasing fugitives did not exceed the ranks;
therefore, there was no disorder.
The strength of the army
lay in not losing the order of the ranks,
not exhausting the strength of men and horses,
and ensuring that slowness and speed did not exceed the commands.
In ancient times,
state decorum did not enter the army,
and military decorum did not enter the state.
If military decorum entered the state, the virtue of the people would be abandoned;
if state decorum entered the army, the virtue of the people would be weakened.
Therefore, in the state, speech was refined and words were gentle.
In the court, there was reverence and humility,
cultivating oneself to treat others,
not arriving unless summoned,
not speaking unless asked,
difficult to advance but easy to retreat.
In the army, one stood firm;
on the march, one was decisive and resolute;
armored warriors did not bow,
war chariots did not salute,
one did not rush on the city walls,
and one did not speak of dangerous matters.
Therefore, ritual and law
are the outer and inner aspects;
culture and martial prowess
approximately.
In ancient times,
wise kings illuminated the people's virtues
and exhausted the people's goodness,
therefore there was no abandonment of virtue
and no disregard of the people.
Rewards had no cause to arise,
punishments had no occasion to be tested.
The Yǒu Yú Shì 有虞氏 (the reign of Emperor Shun) did not reward or punish, yet the people were usable—
this was the utmost virtue.
The Xià 夏 dynasty rewarded but did not punish—
this was the utmost instruction.
The Yīn 殷 dynasty punished but did not reward—
this was the utmost authority.
The Zhōu 周 dynasty used both rewards and punishments—
virtue had declined.
Rewards did not exceed the appropriate time;
this was to make the people quickly obtain the benefit of doing good.
Punishments did not delay in being carried out;
this was to make the people quickly see the harm of doing evil.
Great victories were not rewarded;
both superiors and inferiors did not boast of their goodness.
If superiors did not boast of their goodness,
then they would not be arrogant;
if inferiors did not boast of their goodness,
then ranks would certainly disappear.
When superiors and inferiors do not boast of their goodness like this,
This is the ultimate in yielding.
Even in a great defeat, no one is punished;
superiors and inferiors all consider the fault to lie with themselves.
If superiors truly believe the fault lies with themselves,
they will surely regret their mistakes;
if inferiors truly believe the fault lies with themselves,
they will surely stay far from wrongdoings.
When superiors and inferiors share the blame in this way,
this is the ultimate in yielding.
In ancient times,
garrison troops were not mobilized for three years,
in consideration of the people's hardship.
When superiors and inferiors reciprocate each other in this way,
this is the ultimate in harmony.
Upon achieving victory, they sing songs of triumph,
to show their joy.
They rest at the Líng Tái,
to repay the people's labor,
to show repose.
<Establishing Ranks>
3 *Dìng Jué* (Establishing Ranks)
In all battles, establish ranks and positions,
record merits and crimes,
recruit wandering scholars,
promulgate teachings and proclamations,
interrogate the multitudes,
Seek their skills;
Plan to understand things thoroughly;
Resolve doubts and dismiss suspicions;
Nurture strength and seek cleverness;
Act in accordance with the heart's movements.
In all battles, ensure the many mutually benefit;
Govern chaos and manage advance and retreat;
Submit to righteousness and establish shame;
Simplify laws and reduce punishments.
Execute for minor crimes;
Punish minor offenses severely;
Deal with major crimes according to circumstances.
Obeying Heaven, enriching wealth, pleasing the multitude, benefiting the land, and valuing the army,
these are called the five considerations.
Obey Heaven and follow the seasons;
Enrich wealth by taking advantage of the enemy;
Please the multitude with diligent appearance;
Benefit the land by defending narrow passes and dangerous obstacles;
Value the army by using bows and arrows for defense, spears and lances for guarding, and dagger-axes and halberds for assistance.
In all, the five weapons should employ the long to defend the short,
and the short to rescue the long;
Alternating battles will last long;
Engaging in all-out battles will be strong;
Observe things and plan accordingly;
This is called "twofold advantage."
The ruler should appear diligent,
Observe the enemy and then act.
The general's mind,
that is the mind;
the minds of the multitude,
that is also the mind.
Horses, oxen, chariots, soldiers rested and well-fed,
that is strength.
Teaching should be thorough beforehand, fighting should be disciplined.
The general,
that is the body;
the soldiers,
that is the limbs;
the squad,
that is the fingers and thumbs.
In all battles, wisdom is key;
individual combat,
courage is key;
formations,
skill is key.
Employ what they desire,
perform what they are capable of,
discard what they do not desire and are not capable of,
do the opposite to the enemy.
In all battles there is *tiān* (天, heavenly timing), there is wealth, and there is goodness.
If the time and day are unpropitious,
divination favors victory while conduct is secretive,
This is called possessing *tiān* (natural order).
Having resources,
having,
consequently producing beauty,
this is called possessing *cái* (wealth).
People are accustomed to deploying advantages in battle formations,
exhausting resources in preparations,
this is called possessing *shàn* (goodness/skill).
People are encouraged to reach their responsibilities,
this is called delighting the people.
A large army is for strengthening defense,
much strength is for causing weariness (to the enemy).
Being capable with resources and simplifying governance,
observing things and responding swiftly,
this is called performing preparations.
Light chariots and light infantry,
bows and arrows firmly defending,
this is called a large army.
Secrecy and stillness with much inner strength,
this is called a firm formation.
Advancing and retreating based on this,
this is called much strength.
Superiors having leisure to teach people,
this is called a wearisome formation.
Being natural and having occupation,
this is called being capable with resources.
Distinguishing things based on this,
this is called simplifying governance.
Assess the numbers of the multitude and adapt to the terrain;
Deploy formations according to the enemy's situation;
In attack and battle, defense and advance, retreat and halt,
maintain order between front and rear;
Coordinate chariots and infantry;
This is called "War Participation."
Disobedience, disbelief, discord, idleness, doubt, weariness, fear, fragmentation, resistance, submission, hesitation, recklessness, collapse, slowness,
these are called "War Calamities."
Arrogance, timidity, lamentation, apprehension, regret,
these are called "Ruin and Failure."
Size, strength and weakness, mingling of units, many and few, these two extremes,
these are called "War Weighing."
In all battles, observe the distant and examine the near;
Adapt to the times and consider resources;
Value trust and despise doubt;
Wage war justly;
Act at the right time;
Treat people with kindness.
When you see the enemy is calm,
and when you see chaos, create leisure;
When you see danger and difficulty, do not forget your troops.
In governing the state, show kindness with trust;
In the army, be broad with martial prowess;
On the edge of the blade, be decisive and quick.
In governing the state, be harmonious;
In the army, use law;
Observe the blade's edge;
in the state, observe what is favored;
in the army, observe the square formations;
on the blade's edge, observe trustworthiness.
In general, the deployment of formations should be sparse,
fighting should be dense,
and troops should be diverse.
When instruction is thorough,
tranquility leads to order,
and authority and benefit are clear.
If ministers adhere to righteousness, then the people are encouraged;
if careful consideration leads to success, then the people are convinced.
When the timing is right, then submit to the order;
when things are clear,
the eyes are sharp;
when deliberation is settled,
the heart is strong;
advance and retreat without doubt,
face the enemy without scheming,
listen for execution without questioning who is to be named,
do not change the flag.
In general, good deeds will grow,
and following the ancient ways will lead to success.
If oaths are clear, people are strengthened;
eliminate evil omens.
The way to eliminate evil:
First is righteousness (yì),
cover it with trustworthiness (xìn),
approach it with strength (qiáng),
thereby forming the basis for unifying all under Heaven (tiānxià),
and people will be pleased.
This is called employing the people completely.
First is authority (quán),
fulfilling their excess,
depriving them of their desires,
I from their outside,
act from their inside.
First is people (rén),
second is uprightness (zhèng),
third is rhetoric (cí),
fourth is skill (qiǎo),
fifth is fire (huǒ),
sixth is water (shuǐ),
seventh is arms (bīng).
These are called the Seven Governances (qīzhèng).
Honor (róng), profit (lì), shame (chǐ), death (sǐ),
these are called the Four Guards (sìshǒu).
Dignified appearance and accumulated authority
are nothing more than changing one's intention,
all of this is the Way (dào).
Only the benevolent (rén) have affection,
to have benevolence (rén) without trustworthiness (xìn)
will lead to one's own downfall.
Rén rén, zhèng zhèng, cí cí, huǒ huǒ.
Generally speaking, the way of war
first establishes its spirit,
then issues its orders,
influences it with appearances,
guides it with words.
Use fear to warn,
use desire to motivate,
tread upon the enemy, control the land,
and assign tasks according to their abilities;
this is called the art of war.
Generally, people's behavior
depends on what the masses seek.
Test them by assigning tasks,
and they will surely perform them well.
If they act improperly,
the commander must hold himself accountable.
If they act properly,
constantly remind them not to forget.
Repeat these steps three times, and it will become a pattern.
The principles of life
are called the law.
Generally speaking, the principles of governing chaos and order are:
first, benevolence (rén);
second, trustworthiness (xìn);
third, uprightness (zhí);
Four is called "unity" (yī),
five is called "righteousness" (yì),
six is called "change" (biàn),
seven is called "respect" (zūn).
Establishing law,
first is called "acceptance" (shòu),
second is called "law" (fǎ),
third is called "establishment" (lì),
fourth is called "swiftness" (jí),
fifth is called "controlling their clothing" (yù qí fú),
sixth is called "equalizing their colors" (děng qí sè),
seventh is called "all officials should not have excessive clothing" (bǎi guān yí wú yín fú).
In general, in military missions, if the law rests with oneself, it is called "specialization" (zhuān),
if inferiors fear the law, it is called "law" (fǎ),
the army should not listen to trivial matters,
in battle there should be no small gains,
daily accomplishments and subtle actions are called "the way" (dào).
In general, in battle, if the standards are not consistent, affairs become specialized (zhuān),
if they do not obey, then there is law (fǎ),
if they do not trust each other, then there is unity (yī).
If there is negligence, then stir them up (dòng zhī),
if there is doubt, then change it (biàn zhī),
if the people do not trust their superiors, then carry out actions that will not be repeated,
this has been the policy since ancient times.
〈Yán Wèi〉
4 *Yán Wèi*
Generally, the principles of warfare are:
Positions should be strict,
discipline should be stern,
strength should be deep and unfathomable,
morale should be relaxed,
minds should be unified.
Generally, the principles of warfare are:
Equalize moral principles,
establish squads and companies,
fix formations and ranks,
rectify vertical and horizontal alignments,
examine names and realities.
When advancing, stoop;
when sitting, advance on your knees;
when fearful, stay close;
when in danger, sit.
Those at a distance, observing, will not fear;
those nearby, if not watched, will not scatter.
If the position is beneath, to the left, or to the right,
the lower armored soldiers should sit.
Make oaths while slowly advancing.
If the position reaches the foot soldiers,
calculate with considerations of lightness and weight.
Rouse the horses and make noise among the foot soldiers;
when fearful, also keep them close.
Kneeling, sitting, squatting, or prostrating, then advance on your knees and give oaths broadly.
Starting with shouts and drums, advance, then stop them with the *duó* (鐸, large bell).
Holding gags in their mouths, they swear to be prepared;
sitting on their knees, they advance it.
When executing punishments, forbid looking back;
make an uproar to precede it.
If they are excessively fearful,
then do not execute them;
show them your countenance,
tell them the reasons for their survival,
and carefully examine their duties.
Generally, the soldiers of the three armies should be on alert every day,
and the people should not be allowed to rest.
They should not be allowed to eat separately.
When they are confused and uncertain,
they can be taught and subdued.
In general, battles are prolonged by strength,
but won by morale;
they are prolonged by stability,
but won by danger;
a firm foundation leads to stability,
fresh morale leads to victory;
strong armor leads to stability,
superior weaponry leads to victory.
Generally, chariots rely on compactness for stability,
infantry rely on sitting (remaining in position) for stability,
armor relies on weight for stability,
weapons rely on lightness for victory.
When people have a desire to win,
they only see the enemy.
When people have a fearful heart,
they only see what they fear.
When both hearts are firmly set,
the benefits of both are as one.
The duties of both are performed,
and it is only by authority that they are observed.
In general, in war, moving lightly, lightly is dangerous;
moving heavily, heavily results in no accomplishment;
moving lightly but regarding it as heavy leads to defeat;
moving heavily but regarding it as light leads to battle.
Therefore, in war, lightness and heaviness are relative.
Discard meticulous armor and weapons,
the arrangement of formations and ranks,
and in battle be meticulous about advancing and halting.
In general, in war, respect leads to satisfaction;
leadership leads to submission;
when the superior is troubled, value lightness;
when the superior is at leisure, value heaviness;
a quick drumbeat means lightness;
a slow drumbeat means heaviness;
simple clothing means lightness;
beautiful clothing means heaviness.
In general, when chariots are sturdy
and armor and weapons are sharp,
Lightness is the root of heaviness.
If the superiors are all the same, there will be no gains;
if the superiors are solely self-willed, there will be much death;
if the superiors are indecisive, there will be much doubt;
if the superiors seek death, they will not prevail.
Ordinary men die for love,
die for anger,
die for prestige,
die for righteousness,
die for profit.
The way of war is such that,
instruction induces men to treat death lightly,
principle induces men to die uprightly.
In all battles, there are victories,
defeats,
(factors dependent on) Heaven,
(factors dependent on) man.
In all battles, the precautions for the three armies should not exceed three days;
the warnings to one soldier should not exceed a portion of a day;
the prohibitions for one man should not exceed a full rest.
In all great excellence, use the root;
secondarily, use the branches;
grasp the strategy, defend the subtle;
root and branch are solely matters of weighing [circumstances];
this is war.
In all cases of defeating an army, one person's victory is key.
In all drum signals:
drum for the banners and flags,
drum for the chariots,
drum for the horses,
drum for the infantry,
drum for the soldiers,
drum for the head (command),
drum for the feet (movement),
drum for combined unity.
In all battles, once consolidated, do not attack repeatedly;
in repeated advances, do not exhaust your forces;
in all cases, exhaustion is dangerous.
In all battles, arranging the formation (zhèn) is not difficult,
making men able to arrange the formation is difficult;
making them able to arrange the formation is not difficult,
making men able to use it is difficult;
knowing it is not difficult,
implementing it is difficult.
People have inherent nature (xìng);
nature varies by region (zhōu);
education forms customs (sú);
customs vary by region;
principle (dào) transforms customs.
In all situations of many versus few,
even having won, act as if you haven't.
Weapons do not proclaim their sharpness,
armor does not proclaim its sturdiness,
chariots do not proclaim their solidity,
horses do not proclaim their quality,
the masses do not boast of their numbers—
one has not grasped the Dao
In general, if one wins a battle, then share the benefits with the masses.
If the general is to fight again,
then emphasize rewards and punishments.
If he causes the battle to be lost,
then take the blame upon himself.
In a renewed battle,
then vow to be at the front.
Abandon previous tactics,
whether victorious or not, do not revert to them.
This is called the correct principle.
Generally, the people are saved by rén (仁),
they fight with yì (義),
they decide with zhì (智),
they struggle with yǒng (勇),
they are committed with xìn (信),
they are encouraged by lì (利),
they conquer with gōng (功).
Therefore, to have rén (仁) in the heart,
to practice yì (義) in action,
is to be capable of understanding things with zhì (智),
Able to employ great courage,
able to maintain long-term trust.
Yielding promotes harmony,
people become harmonious.
Starting from oneself, do not be inflexible,
contend for worthies to achieve,

In all battles, strike at their subtle stillness,
avoid their strong stillness;

<Employing the Masses>
5 《Employing the Masses》
Generally, the way of battle is
to use a small force for consolidation,
to use a large force for governance,
a small force benefits from being complex,
a large force benefits from being straightforward.
Use a large force to advance and halt,
use a small force to advance and retreat.
When a large force surrounds a small one,
then encircle from afar and leave an opening.
If dividing and attacking in turn,
To await a multitude with a few,
if the multitude is suspicious,
then rely on yourself.
If someone appropriates benefits, then lower the flag,
meet them and turn them back.
If the enemy is numerous, then appear numerous and accept being surrounded.
If the enemy is few or fearful,
then avoid them and open up a path.
In all battles, face away from the wind and away from high ground.
Have high ground on the right, and danger on the left.
Scout the Pèi (沛) River and the Yí (圯) River.
Use both open camps and encircling tortoise formations.
In all battles, deploy and observe their actions.
Watch the enemy and then act,
if waiting, then advance slowly without beating the drums,
wait for the actions of the multitude.
If attacking, then encamp and watch them.
In all battles, observe changes based on the size of the force,
observe their considerations based on their laxity,
observe their stability based on their advances and retreats,
observe their fear based on their danger,
observe their negligence based on their stillness,
observe their doubts based on their movements,
observe their governance based on their ambushes.
Strike at their doubts,
increase their exhaustion,
Cause them to yield;
attack their plans.
Taking advantage of their lack of defense,
obstruct their designs,
seize their considerations,
capitalize on their fears.
Whenever pursuing a fleeing enemy, do not cease;
if the enemy perhaps stops on the road, then be wary of this.
Whenever nearing an enemy capital,
there must be a path for advance,
retreat must have plans for return.
In general, to fight first leads to exhaustion,
to fight later leads to intimidation,
to rest leads to indolence,
not resting also leads to exhaustion,
resting for a long time will also reverse their intimidation.
Severing letters and trusted relationships,
this is called cutting off the enemy's concerns for its allies.
Selecting good soldiers and arraying the troops accordingly,
this is called increasing one's strength by benefiting the people.
Abandoning responsibilities and economizing on food,
this is called discerning the intentions of the people,
this is the policy of ancient times.
